title: Swap Activity Rate Trending
exclusions: Detects a sustained rise in host-level Linux swap-out rate derived from the cumulative `pgSwapOut` field in the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux `vmstat` event source. It does not measure swap-in, combine the native `vmstat(8)` `si` and `so` display columns, convert pages to bytes without a measured page size, prove swap thrashing or application impact, identify a responsible process or cgroup, monitor containers independently of the host procfs namespace, or treat swap occupancy as activity. Counter resets and gaps are rejected, but this source has no boot ID and cannot conclusively separate a rapid post-reboot counter from the preceding boot. The primary SPL applies no hidden maintenance exclusion and makes no security, compliance, prevention, or production-validation claim.
evidence: After deployment, retain the versioned `linux_swapout_rate_trend_15m` saved-search definition and schedule, effective `vmstat.sh` input and search-time configuration, source-health report, triggered result rows, dashboard export, threshold approval, and dated positive, negative, reset, and gap control outputs. Each finding should preserve `host`, `window_start`, `window_end`, `baseline_buckets`, `observed_buckets`, `breach_buckets`, `prior_hour_avg_pages_per_second`, `minimum_swapout_pages_per_second`, `average_swapout_pages_per_second`, `current_swapout_pages_per_second`, `peak_swapout_pages_per_second`, `threshold_pages_per_second`, and `current_swap_used_pct`. These artifacts show what the configured counter feed and search reported; this documentation-only review produced no indexed fixture, runtime result, production evidence, or operator sign-off.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Fix `now()` to a five-minute boundary and index one numeric `index=os source=vmstat sourcetype=vmstat` event per minute for `host=swap-trend-positive`, beginning five minutes before the 60-minute baseline and ending at the last minute of the three closed candidate buckets. Increase cumulative `pgSwapOut` by 60 pages per 60-second interval throughout all 12 baseline buckets, then by 600 pages per interval in each of the three candidate buckets; keep `swapUsedPct=20`. The derived rates must be 1 and 10 pages/second respectively. Expect one result with `baseline_buckets=12`, `observed_buckets=3`, `breach_buckets=3`, `prior_hour_avg_pages_per_second=1`, `threshold_pages_per_second=4`, and candidate minimum, average, current, and peak rates equal to 10 pages/second.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Repeat the fixed-time fixture for `host=swap-trend-negative` with the same 1-page/second baseline and 10 pages/second in only the first two candidate buckets; return to 1 page/second in the third. Expect no final row because `breach_buckets=2`. Test guards separately by decreasing `pgSwapOut`, inserting a sample gap greater than 180 seconds, omitting enough samples to leave fewer than four valid rates in one candidate bucket, setting `pgSwapOut=?`, and duplicating an exact host/timestamp event. A reset, long gap, malformed value, incomplete bucket, or duplicate must not create a qualifying trend.

dataSources: Primary source: complete `index=os source=vmstat sourcetype=vmstat` events produced once per minute by the supplied `vmstat.sh` scripted event input in the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833). Required fields are `_time`, `host`, and numeric cumulative `pgSwapOut`; numeric `swapUsedPct` is optional context. On Linux the add-on derives `pgSwapOut` from the `vmstat -s` pages-swapped-out counter. `os`, `source=vmstat`, and the 60-second interval are explicit deployment conventions and must be changed consistently if local configuration differs.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833), installed on the Linux collection forwarders that execute `vmstat.sh` and on the Splunk tiers required for its parsing and search-time knowledge. A Universal Forwarder transports the data but is not Splunkbase app 617 and is not itself the field contract.

splunkbaseApps.name: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux

spl:
index=os source=vmstat sourcetype=vmstat host=* earliest=-90m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval pgSwapOut=tonumber(pgSwapOut), swapUsedPct=tonumber(swapUsedPct)
| where isnotnull(pgSwapOut) AND pgSwapOut>=0
| stats max(pgSwapOut) as pgSwapOut latest(swapUsedPct) as swapUsedPct by host _time
| sort 0 host _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(pgSwapOut) as previous_pgSwapOut last(_time) as previous_time by host
| eval elapsed_seconds=_time-previous_time
| eval swapout_delta_pages=if(pgSwapOut>=previous_pgSwapOut,pgSwapOut-previous_pgSwapOut,null())
| eval swapout_pages_per_second=if(elapsed_seconds>0 AND elapsed_seconds<=180,swapout_delta_pages/elapsed_seconds,null())
| where isnotnull(swapout_pages_per_second)
| bin _time span=5m
| stats avg(swapout_pages_per_second) as swapout_pages_per_second max(swapout_pages_per_second) as peak_swapout_pages_per_second count as rate_samples latest(swapUsedPct) as swap_used_pct by host _time
| where rate_samples>=4
| eval baseline_start=relative_time(now(),"-80m@m"), candidate_start=relative_time(now(),"-20m@m"), candidate_end=relative_time(now(),"-5m@m")
| eval baseline_rate=if(_time>=baseline_start AND _time<candidate_start,swapout_pages_per_second,null())
| eventstats avg(baseline_rate) as prior_hour_avg_pages_per_second count(baseline_rate) as baseline_buckets by host
| where _time>=candidate_start AND _time<candidate_end
| eval threshold_pages_per_second=max(4,2*prior_hour_avg_pages_per_second), breached=if(swapout_pages_per_second>=threshold_pages_per_second,1,0)
| sort 0 host _time
| stats count as observed_buckets sum(breached) as breach_buckets min(_time) as window_start max(_time) as window_end min(swapout_pages_per_second) as minimum_swapout_pages_per_second avg(swapout_pages_per_second) as average_swapout_pages_per_second latest(swapout_pages_per_second) as current_swapout_pages_per_second max(peak_swapout_pages_per_second) as peak_swapout_pages_per_second latest(swap_used_pct) as current_swap_used_pct latest(prior_hour_avg_pages_per_second) as prior_hour_avg_pages_per_second latest(baseline_buckets) as baseline_buckets latest(threshold_pages_per_second) as threshold_pages_per_second by host
| where baseline_buckets>=9 AND observed_buckets=3 AND breach_buckets=3
| eval window_end=window_end+300, minimum_swapout_pages_per_second=round(minimum_swapout_pages_per_second,2), average_swapout_pages_per_second=round(average_swapout_pages_per_second,2), current_swapout_pages_per_second=round(current_swapout_pages_per_second,2), peak_swapout_pages_per_second=round(peak_swapout_pages_per_second,2), prior_hour_avg_pages_per_second=round(prior_hour_avg_pages_per_second,2), threshold_pages_per_second=round(threshold_pages_per_second,2), current_swap_used_pct=round(current_swap_used_pct,1), severity="medium"
| sort 0 -average_swapout_pages_per_second host
| table host severity window_start window_end baseline_buckets observed_buckets breach_buckets prior_hour_avg_pages_per_second minimum_swapout_pages_per_second average_swapout_pages_per_second current_swapout_pages_per_second peak_swapout_pages_per_second threshold_pages_per_second current_swap_used_pct
description: Reports a Linux host when all three recent closed five-minute buckets have at least four valid swap-out rates and average at least both 4 pages/second and twice the host's prior-hour average. The search derives pages/second from adjacent cumulative `pgSwapOut` observations, rejects decreases and gaps longer than 180 seconds, and requires at least nine complete baseline buckets. “Trend” means a sustained departure from the preceding hour, not a claim that every individual sample rises monotonically.
value: Sustained swap-out means the kernel is repeatedly evicting memory pages to swap, which can precede storage contention, later swap-in latency, and workload degradation. Comparing a complete recent window with the same host's prior hour gives Linux operators a unit-safe early investigation signal without confusing an ever-growing lifetime counter or an old swap allocation with current activity.
implementation: Deploy Splunkbase 833 to the required collection and search tiers, enable its supplied `vmstat.sh` event input at 60-second cadence into the approved operating-system event index, and verify complete events with numeric `pgSwapOut`. Save `linux_swapout_rate_trend_15m`, schedule it every five minutes on bucket boundaries, and retain the explicit delayed window. Start with the documented floor of 4 pages/second and two-times baseline in all three candidate buckets; baseline and approve thresholds by host class because neither Linux nor Splunk prescribes them.
visualization: Plot per-host five-minute `swapout_pages_per_second` with the prior-hour average and resolved threshold on an axis explicitly labelled `pages/second`. Add a latest-first finding table containing every evidence field, a separate `swapUsedPct` occupancy panel, and a source-health panel for missing events, `?` values, duplicate timestamps, counter decreases, and stale hosts. Provide same-host drilldowns to memory availability, major faults, pressure-stall information, storage latency, OOM events, process/cgroup memory, deployments, and reboots. Never graph raw `pgSwapOut` as a rate, label pages/second as bytes/second, or mix pages/second and percentage on an unlabelled axis.
dataModelAcceleration: No exact accelerated CIM search is asserted. The Performance.Memory model defines memory and swap capacity in megabytes, including `swap_used`, but it does not preserve the source-specific cumulative `pgSwapOut` page counter, adjacent sample time, reset/gap guards, or derived pages/second. CIM memory panels can supply occupancy context only; substituting swap-used percentage would change this detector's meaning.

knownFalsePositives:
Every qualifying result represents a real increase in the indexed cumulative counter under this source contract, but the increase may be expected, harmless for the workload, or distorted by collection identity.

1. **Approved stress-ng memory or swap qualification** — A resilience or capacity test can intentionally drive sustained page-out. Match the exact host, test command/job, UTC window, owner, and change record. Preserve the finding as test evidence and suppress notification delivery only for that bounded window.

2. **Database, JVM, or application cache warm-up and rebalance** — PostgreSQL, Oracle, Elasticsearch, Spark, or a large Java service can temporarily force older anonymous pages toward swap after a restart or working-set shift. Correlate the service lifecycle, resident memory, major faults, swap-in, pressure stalls, storage latency, and user objective before deciding the activity is benign.

3. **Nightly batch, backup, restore, or analytics phase** — Veeam agents, rsync, compression, ETL, and report generation can create a repeatable memory peak. Confirm the scheduler job and normal duration. Use a separate reviewed host-class threshold or exact job window; do not permanently exclude every batch host.

4. **Virtual-machine ballooning, migration, or host overcommit** — Hypervisor reclamation can make the guest kernel evict pages even though the guest workload did not change. Correlate guest findings with balloon size, reservation, migration, and physical-host telemetry. The guest counter proves page-out, not which virtualization policy caused it.

5. **Reboot, suspend/resume, cloned hostname, or duplicate collector** — `pgSwapOut` normally falls on reboot and the SPL discards the decreasing pair, but the source lacks a boot ID. A rapid new counter that exceeds a low old value, two systems sharing `host`, or two enabled stanzas can produce unsafe adjacency. Compare boot/uptime events, forwarder GUID, source, `_indextime`, and per-minute counts; repair identity or deployment rather than suppressing the symptom.

6. **Baseline mismatch after resize or permanent workload change** — The prior hour may be unrepresentative immediately after RAM, swap, kernel, image, or workload changes. Require at least nine complete baseline buckets, correlate the approved change, and rebaseline by governed host class. Do not remove completeness, reset, or gap checks to make a new baseline converge faster.

7. **Four-pages/second floor unsuitable for the host** — Because the add-on source does not publish page size, four pages/second is intentionally a page-count policy, not 16 KiB/s or another byte rate. Review the floor against measured page size, service latency, storage, and workload class. If byte-rate policy is required, collect page size in a separate tested source contract rather than relabelling this field.

**Safe suppression:** keep the catalogue SPL unchanged and apply any local exception after the final result through a deployment-managed lookup such as `linux_capacity_exceptions.csv`. Use an exact `host` plus numeric `valid_from_epoch`, `valid_until_epoch`, owner, reason, ticket, and approver; reject wildcards, duplicate keys, and non-expiring rows. Keep suppressed matches visible for review. Never suppress raw events before `streamstats`, because removing samples can splice unrelated cumulative observations, and never suppress missing-data, malformed-field, duplicate-source, or reset health findings.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational Linux memory-performance monitoring; no adversary behavior is asserted)

cost.search_load_notes: Five-minute scheduled raw-event search over roughly 85 minutes of one compact vmstat event per host per minute; streamstats and sort scale with host count.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact measurement contract

Assign a Linux platform owner, a Splunk collection/content owner, and a workload escalation path. Use a supported Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux release and qualify it against the deployment's Linux, Universal Forwarder, parsing-tier, search-tier, and Splunk Cloud or Enterprise versions. Install the add-on where Splunk's topology guidance requires its scripts, parsing configuration, and search-time knowledge. The search role needs read access to the selected operating-system event index and permission to schedule the saved search; alert-action and app-administration rights should remain separate. Splunk's add-on documentation states that its scripts require execute permission and documents root execution for supported collection. Assess that requirement under local security policy rather than granting ad hoc unrestricted sudo or editing vendor scripts.

Preserve the signal distinction. On Linux, the add-on's `vmstat.sh` summary event exposes `pgSwapOut`, derived from the `vmstat -s` pages-swapped-out counter. It is a cumulative page count, normally increasing for the lifetime of a boot. It is not pages per collection interval, not pages/second, and not the periodic native command's `so` field. The procps-ng manual defines `si` and `so` as rates and notes that the first periodic report is an average since reboot; this sidecar does not search those display columns. The rate here is `(current_pgSwapOut-previous_pgSwapOut)/(current_event_time-previous_event_time)` and its unit is pages/second.

Do not convert that result to bytes, kB, KB, KiB, or MiB unless the same event contract measures and preserves the host's page size. A common 4,096-byte page is not a safe catalogue-wide constant. `swapUsedPct` is an instantaneous occupancy gauge and is carried only as context. A host can have allocated swap with no current page-out, or active page-out while occupancy changes slowly. Swap-out alone also does not prove thrashing; that stronger diagnosis needs swap-in plus impact evidence such as pressure stalls, major faults, storage latency, and application symptoms.

The catalogue names the index `os`, source `vmstat`, source type `vmstat`, cadence 60 seconds, saved search `linux_swapout_rate_trend_15m`, and initial floor 4 pages/second. These are deployment contracts, not vendor defaults or universal thresholds. Change them consistently in input, SPL, dashboard, tests, roles, and runbook. This use case intentionally complements UC-1.1.100, which defines a separate page-size-aware custom source for swap-in; do not merge fields from the two event contracts by name alone.

## Step 1 — Configure and qualify the supplied vmstat event input

On a deployment app, create or update `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_nix/local/inputs.conf`. Copy only the installed release's existing `vmstat.sh` stanza from `default/inputs.conf`; do not copy the whole default file, modify `bin/vmstat.sh`, or invent a script path. A typical local override is:

```ini
[script://./bin/vmstat.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = 60
index = os
source = vmstat
sourcetype = vmstat
```

Deploy through the approved forwarder-management path and restart the Splunk process when required by the documented workflow. Verify the winning stanza with `splunk btool inputs list --debug` on a representative collector. Run the add-on's supported diagnostic mode if available in the installed release and inspect `splunkd.log` for the exact script path when execution fails. Do not enable both an event and a duplicate local copy of the same script.

At 60 seconds, expect about 1,440 complete multiline events per host per day. Measure actual serialized bytes and license effect on canaries; event count is not a byte estimate. Search `index=os source=vmstat sourcetype=vmstat earliest=-15m` and require approximately one event per minute per host with numeric `_time`, `host`, `pgSwapOut`, and preferably `swapUsedPct`. The add-on emits `?` for unavailable values, so `tonumber` returning null is a source-health condition rather than zero activity. If an Edge or Ingest Processor vmstat-reduction template is used, preserve `pgSwapOut`; Splunk's published template can remove or replace selected vmstat fields and requires complete events.

On two representative Linux hosts, compare the newest indexed `pgSwapOut` with the `pages swapped out` line from `vmstat -s` at nearly the same time. Also inspect `pswpout` in `/proc/vmstat` where approved. On a full Splunk Enterprise collector, compare the effective stanza with Splunk Web > Settings > Data inputs > Scripts and confirm that the `vmstat.sh` row is enabled with the intended interval and index; a Universal Forwarder has no Splunk Web, so use `btool` there. Allow for collection and forwarding delay, but confirm counter direction and scale. Record `_indextime-_time` percentiles and per-minute counts. A host with no event, a `?` value, or material lateness is unknown, not a zero rate.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the saved search

Save the primary SPL as `linux_swapout_rate_trend_15m` and schedule it with cron `*/5 * * * *`. Trigger when result count is greater than zero. Keep `earliest=-90m@m latest=-5m@m`: the search excludes the current and immediately preceding open/late interval, retains one predecessor before the 60-minute baseline, and evaluates three closed five-minute candidate buckets. Measure real ingest lag and lengthen the delay if late events routinely miss the window.

The first `eval` converts `pgSwapOut` and optional occupancy to numbers. The `where` rejects `?`, missing, and negative counters. `stats max(pgSwapOut) by host _time` collapses exact duplicate timestamps without summing a cumulative counter; duplicate-source health must still be monitored separately. `sort 0 host _time` is mandatory before `streamstats`, which carries the immediately preceding observation for that host.

`elapsed_seconds` uses observed event time, not an assumed 60. A nondecreasing counter yields `swapout_delta_pages`; a decrease becomes null because it may represent reboot, reset, hostname collision, or malformed data. Only positive elapsed intervals no greater than 180 seconds become rates. The gap cap prevents an hour of cumulative page-out from being divided down and presented as recent activity. Because the source has no boot ID, the decrease check cannot detect every cross-boot comparison; boot and identity health remain separate controls.

Five-minute buckets average valid adjacent rates, retain their peak, and require at least four rates. This tolerates one missing minute without allowing a sparse point to represent five minutes. The prior-hour baseline contains up to 12 complete buckets; at least nine are required. Candidate buckets are the three closed intervals from 20 through 5 minutes before dispatch. Each candidate must meet `max(4 pages/second, 2 * prior-hour average)`, and all three must breach. Thus the rule describes a sustained 15-minute departure from recent behavior. It does not require every one-minute rate to rise, and `trend` must not be described as monotonic acceleration.

The absolute floor prevents a zero or tiny baseline from making negligible activity alertable. Four pages/second and the two-times factor are transparent catalogue starting policy, not Linux, procps-ng, or Splunk recommendations. Baseline database, web, analytics, virtual-desktop, and batch hosts separately. If the organization needs a byte-rate policy, extend collection to include a validated page-size field and revise SPL, fields, controls, dashboard labels, and evidence together; never multiply by an assumed 4 KiB in a display.

The optional `swapUsedPct` result helps triage occupancy but does not gate the alert. There is no equivalent CIM `tstats` detector: CIM Performance.Memory has swap capacity gauges in megabytes, not this cumulative source counter and its adjacent timing. Trigger per result, route to Linux operations, throttle notifications by host for at least the evaluated window, and retain every scheduled finding. Do not automatically kill a process, drop caches, disable swap, change swappiness, restart a service, or resize a host.

## Step 3 — Validate units, windows, and guard behavior

First validate one real pair by hand: subtract older `pgSwapOut` from newer, divide by the exact `_time` difference in seconds, and compare with `swapout_pages_per_second` before bucketing. If 600 pages accumulate over 60 seconds, the result is 10 pages/second; it is not 600 pages/second, 10 KiB/s, or 40 KiB/s. Compare directionally with a second delayed `vmstat` report only after checking the installed command's selected units and interval. Do not compare the cumulative `vmstat -s` number directly to periodic `so`.

Execute the positive control at fixed absolute event times. Supply one predecessor and 12 complete baseline buckets at 1 page/second, then three complete candidate buckets at 10 pages/second. Confirm that the prior-hour average is 1, the resolved threshold is 4 rather than 2, all three candidate buckets contain at least four rates, and the final result has the exact expected counts and rates. Execute the negative fixture with only two candidate breaches; no row may survive.

Run guard tests independently. A decreasing counter must make only the spanning rate null. A gap of 181 seconds must be rejected. A candidate bucket with three valid rates must be removed and cause `observed_buckets` to fall below three. `pgSwapOut=?` must not become zero. Exact duplicate host/timestamp events must not be summed. Test a host with only eight complete baseline buckets and require no result. Also inspect an actual reboot: the decreasing pair should be discarded, collection should recover on later pairs, and a separate uptime/source-health panel should expose the lifecycle event.

Validate source completeness for at least 24 hours with a one-minute host timechart, latest-event age, null/`?` counts, duplicate host/timestamp counts, counter-decrease counts, and p95/p99 ingest lag. Compare expected Linux inventory with hosts seen in the feed. Absence of a trend result does not prove the source is present or healthy. This editorial pass reviewed arithmetic and source semantics only; it did not run Splunk, index fixture data, execute the saved search, or qualify a production add-on release. Keep `status=draft` until a responsible operator performs and signs the controls.

## Step 4 — Operationalize triage and evidence

Build the panels described in `visualization`. Keep raw counters, derived rates, occupancy percentages, and byte-valued context on separately labelled axes. The primary trend should show five-minute pages/second, the prior-hour average, and the resolved threshold. Add memory availability, swap-in from a separately validated source, major-fault rate, pressure-stall information, block-device latency, OOM messages, and application service objectives for the same host and time range.

The response runbook should: (1) verify complete source events, one collection path, numeric counter, expected cadence, and no reset/gap in the evaluated window; (2) recompute one adjacent rate; (3) confirm reboot, suspend, migration, ballooning, deployment, backup, restore, batch, and load-test context; (4) correlate occupancy, swap-in, pressure, major faults, storage latency, and user impact; (5) identify process and cgroup memory consumers with approved tools; and (6) involve the workload owner before remediation. System-wide page-out cannot identify which process created pressure, and the process currently touching memory may differ from the one that caused earlier eviction.

Retain the artifacts named in `evidence` under local operations policy. Record search revision, threshold revision, add-on release, source-health result, and exception revision with each evidence set. Do not invent a SOC owner, `audit_evidence` index, universal retention period, or compliance claim. These records demonstrate configured monitoring and observed counter behavior only.

Review the baseline and floor after RAM or swap changes, kernel/add-on upgrades, workload migration, virtualization-policy changes, or service-objective revisions. Review source health after parsing or ingest-pipeline changes. Keep a versioned test record for each change.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot and suppress safely

- **No vmstat events:** verify add-on deployment, effective input stanza, script execute rights, the vendor-documented execution identity, index routing, forwarding, and search-role access. Inspect `splunkd.log` for the exact `vmstat.sh` invocation.
- **Events exist but `pgSwapOut` is null or `?`:** confirm a complete multiline event, exact `sourcetype=vmstat`, search-time knowledge on the search tier, supported Linux commands, and any ingest-reduction configuration. Never coalesce this field to zero.
- **All rates are null:** inspect ordering, duplicate timestamps, counter decreases, and gaps over 180 seconds. The first accepted observation per host has no predecessor and is intentionally null.
- **Implausibly large rates:** look for host collisions, duplicate forwarders, clock jumps, stale queued events, a changed field meaning, or merged environments. Compare the two raw counter events before changing thresholds.
- **Visible rate but no alert:** verify at least nine complete baseline buckets, all three candidate buckets, at least four rates per bucket, the 4-pages/second floor, the two-times factor, search alignment, and indexing delay. One or two breached buckets are intentionally insufficient.
- **Counter decreases after reboot:** this is expected lifetime behavior. Confirm the reboot and let later adjacent samples establish a new rate. Do not use `abs(delta)` or convert the drop to activity.
- **Rate disagrees with native vmstat:** distinguish the indexed cumulative summary counter from periodic `so`, align time windows, verify command units, and account for integer display rounding. Reconcile raw `pgSwapOut` before changing SPL.
- **Persistent high trend:** determine whether the threshold is wrong for the host class or whether workload working set, memory leak, overcommit, ballooning, swappiness policy, or swap-device behavior changed. Resolve capacity or workload policy through change control; a permanent exception is not remediation.

Apply suppression only after a complete final result using the bounded contract in `knownFalsePositives`. Preserve unsuppressed findings and source-health alerts. Never filter raw vmstat events before `streamstats`, because deleting a maintenance interval can splice cumulative observations across the omitted period and misstate its rate. Re-run positive, negative, reset, gap, duplicate, baseline-completeness, and arithmetic controls after any relevant change.
grandmaExplanation: We watch whether a Linux server keeps pushing memory onto slower disk space much faster than it did during the previous hour. That warning helps the team investigate growing memory pressure before people notice a slowdown.
